passages.s: His accurate examination of things in consultations, and patient hearing of others.
Fame after life is no better than oblivion.
If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such thing as wrong.
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature, as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer.
Secondly, that it is in thy power, to do nothing against thine own proper God, and inward spirit.
But still that time come, what will content thee?

XXIII Consider how many different things, whether they concern our bodies, or our souls, in a moment of time come to pass in every one of us, and so thou wilt not wonder if many more things or rather all things that are done, can at one time subsist, and coexist in that both one and general, which we call the world.
No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require.
It will suffice to remember, that all things in general are by certain order and appointment: or if it be but few.
Thou hast therefore been confounded in thy course, and henceforth it will be hard for thee to recover the title and credit of a philosopher.
Some of them no sooner dead, than forgotten.
Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them.
And so shalt thou confess, if thou dost observe it.
But thy duty towards the Gods also, it is time thou shouldst acquit thyself of it with more goodness and simplicity.
For these also, these famous soldiers and warlike men, if thou dost look into their minds and opinions, what do they for the most part but hunt after prey?
But generally remember that nothing can hurt a natural citizen, that is not hurtful unto the city itself, nor anything hurt the city, that is not hurtful unto the law itself.
But above all things, how they are forced by their opinions that they hold, to do what they do; and even those things that they do, with what pride and self-conceit they do them.

If all be a mere confusion without any moderator, or governor, then hast thou reason to congratulate thyself; that in such a general flood of confusion thou thyself hast obtained a reasonable faculty, whereby thou mayest govern thine own life and actions.
When quite young he was made administrator of the free cities in Asia, nor is it surprising to find that he made bitter enemies there; indeed, a just ruler was sure to make enemies.
I am always annoyed with phlegm, but to-day I seem to snivel more than usual.
